extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in religion, theology, and freethought (educated lay audience)
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th-century polemical essay (Thomas Paine's Age of Reason, Part I) presenting principles for judging revelations, scriptures, and religious institutions; contains definitional claims and standards for evidence, poetry, and moral appraisal of sacred texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and limitation of revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Revelation when applied to religion means something communicated immediately from God to man; it is revelation to the first person only, and when told to others it becomes hearsay, and therefore cannot obligate others to believe it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine argues it is a contradiction to call second-hand or written reports 'revelation.' Examples invoked include Moses' tables, the Koran, and the Virgin birth: if the communication was not made to me, I am under no obligation to accept it as revelation. This standard is used to reject claims that books or transmitted traditions are divine revelations in the strict sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of evidence required for public miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary public miracles (e.g., resurrection and ascension) require public and ocular demonstration 'equal to all,' not the testimony of a few witnesses, to justify universal belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine contrasts supernatural birth (private, unverifiable) with resurrection/ascension (which, if true, would admit of public demonstration). He rejects accounts resting on 'eight or nine' witnesses and appeals to the example of Thomas demanding ocular and manual proof—arguing the same standard should apply universally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental honesty as moral requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental faithfulness to one's own beliefs is necessary for moral conduct; 'infidelity' is defined as professing to believe what one does not believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine asserts that 'mental lying' (profession of belief contrary to conviction) corrupts character and leads to broader moral decay; he uses priests taking on a trade for gain as an example of perjury leading to other crimes. This serves as an evaluative standard for assessing religious professions and clergy conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revelation cannot be applied to ordinary historical narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Revelation, strictly speaking, cannot claim to cover events witnessed or done upon earth by humans; the anecdotal and historical parts of scriptures are therefore outside the meaning of 'revelation' and cannot be assumed divine on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine reasons that historical stories (e.g., Samson's acts) are either matters of fact or fiction and that revelation does not convert ordinary history into divine communication. This is used to judge much of the Old Testament as tradition or human composition, not revealed scripture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical status does not equal divine authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection of canonical books ('the Word of God') was historically a human, political process — they were 'decided by vote' — and that fact undermines any uncontested claim of divine authority for those books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine notes that the Church collected writings and voted which should be canonical, rejecting others (Apocrypha or doubtful books). He treats that procedure as inadequate external evidence for divine origin and urges examination of internal evidence instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral quality as a criterion for judging scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: The ethical content of sacred writings is a key test: passages that display obscenity, cruelty, vindictiveness, or brutal behavior indicate a text unworthy of being called the 'Word of God.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine contends that much of the Old Testament is 'a history of wickedness' that has corrupted humanity; by this standard he condemns large portions of scripture and praises only certain miscellaneous parts (e.g., Psalms, Job) for elevated sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of poetry (criterion for literary classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry consists principally in two things—imagery and composition (the mixing of long and short syllables); prophesying in scripture often denotes poetic composition rather than literal prophetic revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine offers a technical standard for distinguishing poetry from prose (metrical structure and imagery) and shows prophetic books contain poetical measure. He demonstrates with examples and a short metrical exercise, using this to reclassify prophetic material as poetry rather than revealed literal history.
